newsitem.title: FRANCE: French opposition Socialists say plans block Front.
newsitem.headline: French opposition Socialists say plans block Front.

text.p: France's opposition Socialist party said on Monday it may withdraw one or two candidates from next Sunday's parliamentary election runoffs to help block election of far-right National Front candidates.

Pulling out candidates, under an informal pact among mainstream parties to derail the anti-immigrant Front, would probably hand seats to the ruling centre-right in the June 1 runoff round and weaken the left's chances of overall victory.

"We will stay on each time we can win," party spokesman Francois Hollande told a news conference after the left won a stunning upset in round one on Sunday by winning more votes than the ruling centre-right.

"We will pull out each time that staying on might not only risk a loss for us but a victory for the National Front," Hollande said after a meeting of Socialist leaders to review strategy ahead of the second round.
"It's possible that there may be one or two cases once we have made an even more detailed examination," he said.

The National Front of Jean-Marie Le Pen favours sending home three million immigrants and giving priority to white French people. Polls show his party will probably only win a handful of seats at best.
Hollande said that Socialist candidates in third place might still be able to win in towns with strong National Front support like Orange and Mantes la Jolie.
"When we add up the leftist forces there is a very good chance" of coming from behind for victory, he said.

Official Interior Ministry results showed the combined left polled 40.22 percent of the first-round vote, the centre-right RPR-UDF coalition and other moderate rightists 36.50 percent and the extreme-right National Front 14.94 percent. Ecologists scored 6.81 percent.
The Socialists also planned to send out at least "Seven Musketeers", or senior party politicians, on trips around the country to back up less experienced Socialist candidates before the second round.
The seven included former labour minister Martine Aubry and former culture minister Jack Lang.
Party leader Lionel Jospin travelled to Lyon in central France on Monday for a rally, and would go on to Toulouse in the southwest on Tuesday and to Lille in the north on Wednesday, Hollande said.

He said the Socialists would not seek to resolve glaring differences on European policy with the smaller Communist party ahead of the second round. Jospin would almost certainly have to admit Communists into government.
The two parties signed a pact before the first round pledging to create 700,000 jobs and cut the working week from 39 hours to 35 with no loss of pay.
But they glossed over differences on a single currency -- the Socialists are broadly in favour, the Communists against.
Both parties have a policy of mutually pulling out candidates to enable the best placed to win runoffs.

Under French election rules, a runoff is held between the top two finishers in constituencies where no one wins an absolute majority on the first round. Candidates who win the backing of at least 12.5 percent of the number of registered voters are also eligible for the runoff.
